title: Burst tail analysis: AWQ vs INT8 kernel congestion
content:
Summary / TL;DR:
Observed reproducible 99.9/99.99p tail spikes under short burst workloads when using AWQ kernels vs INT8 kernels on A100-style nodes. Root cause appears to be kernel-level contention and memory bandwidth spikes during microbatch consolidation combined with KV-cache refill paths. AWQ shows slightly better median throughput but worse tail behavior for short, concurrent bursts.

Why I care:
- Customer facing features (chatfront) show intermittent slow responses in production during bursty traffic (CS tickets).
- SLOs require <150ms p99 for single-turn generation for the small-chat endpoint; bursts breach those targets.

Experiment goal:
- Compare AWQ (our optimized AWQ kernels) vs INT8 (reference INT8 kernels) under controlled bursty traffic profiles and identify microarchitectural/serving runtime contributors to the tail.
- Capture stack traces/timers and kernel-level occupancy metrics to decide targeted mitigations (smoothing, prewarm, kernel selection heuristics).

Setup (short):
- HW: 8x A100 40GB (homogeneous), CUDACapacity=high, NIC: 100Gbps
- Runtime: serving-runtime@main@2028-02-01, kernel builds: awq-v2.1 (custom tiling), int8-ref-v1.7
- Model: Llama-2-7B (decoder only), kv-cache warmed in some runs vs cold in others
- Batchpolicy: client microbatching disabled; runtime does continuous batching with 4ms batch window default
- Workload pattern: 50 concurrent clients, 2s on / 3s off per client (spiky), request length: 8 tokens prompt + up to 64 tokens completion, arrival pattern Poisson inside bursts
- Key toggles: kernel=AWQ|INT8, kv_prefetch={on,off}, batching_window={2ms,4ms,8ms}

Metrics captured:
- latency percentiles (p50,p90,p99,p99.9,p99.99)
- per-request kernel selection trace (which kernel chosen, switching events)
- GPU SM occupancy, L2 bandwidth util, DRAM bandwidth util (collected via nvprof/nvtx)
- runtime-level queue length / microbatch size distributions
- kv-cache hit/miss counts and refill latency

Representative numbers (short):
- AWQ, kv_prefetch=on, batch_window=4ms: p50=28ms, p90=65ms, p99=140ms, p99.9=420ms, p99.99=1.8s
- INT8, kv_prefetch=on, batch_window=4ms: p50=32ms, p90=78ms, p99=145ms, p99.9=210ms, p99.99=430ms
- AWQ, kv_prefetch=off, batch_window=4ms: p99.9 spikes to 650ms (kv misses amplified)
- INT8, kv_prefetch=off: p99.9 ~ 260ms

Top-line observation: AWQ gives lower median but significantly worse long tails (p99.9+) vs INT8 in bursty/kV-refill scenarios. In steady-state sustained QPS AWQ is comparable or sometimes better.

Detailed observations & traces: (notes/raw)
- NVTX traces show AWQ kernel launches are more bursty in SM occupancy — there are short periods where one block of SMs is fully saturated while others idle; when multiple requests coincide the launcher queues up additional AWQ kernels rather than merging microbatches effectively.
- INT8 kernel paths are slightly more "merge-friendly" — GPU occupancy ramps smoother and microbatches get aggregated into larger kernel launches more frequently.
- Memory bandwidth graphs: AWQ runs show short, very high (90%+) DRAM bursts at kernel start when kv-cache refills happen; INT8 runs show a more spread-out bandwidth curve. Hypothesis: AWQ uses denser weight layouts with tiled gather that causes concentrated memory access at kernel start.
- KV-cache refill latency: for cold keys, AWQ kernel execution overlaps with refill path poorly — observed a 1-3ms stall per refill on AWQ at high concurrent bursts (multiple refills coincide), while INT8 had 0.5-1ms per refill under similar conditions.
- Host-side latency traces show that AWQ path schedules more small kernels (higher kernel count) for the same request in some sequences (tiling edge-case), increasing scheduler pressure and queueing.

Repro steps (short):
1) Deploy serving-runtime build: main@2028-02-01, kernels in PATH.
2) Start the burst driver (scripts/burst-driver.sh) with args: --concurrency 50 --burst-period 5 --burst-duration 2 --poisson-intensity 10
3) Run two experiments (AWQ vs INT8) with kv_prefetch toggled. Collect nvprof + runtime traces (nvtx on).
4) Pull traces: scripts/collect-traces.sh --run-id <id>

Hypotheses (ranked):
- H1 (high): AWQ kernel layout causes concentrated DRAM bursts on start, which when coincident across requests saturate memory bus and amplify tail.
- H2 (medium): AWQ path emits more smaller kernels for tiled blocks in some sequence lengths, increasing GPU kernel launch overhead and kernel queue contention.
- H3 (low): Prefetching path interacts poorly with AWQ memory access patterns leading to lock-step refills instead of staggered refills.

Small ASCII timeline example from nvtx (excerpt):
[time ms] evt
0.0  client request received
0.3  allocate microbatch  (size 1->2)
2.4  AWQ kernel_A launch -> DRAM burst  (0.5ms)
2.9  AWQ kernel_B launch -> another DRAM burst (0.6ms)
3.0  KV-cache refill start -> stall 1.9ms
4.9  host-side wait for kernel queue -> +6ms

Quick experiments we ran as mitigations (results):
- Increasing batch_window to 8ms reduced AWQ p99.9 from 420ms -> 220ms (good), but p50/p90 increased slightly -> tradeoff between tail and latency for median.
- Enabling a jittered client-side inter-arrival smoothing (add 1-3ms random jitter) reduces worst tail in AWQ runs by ~30%. This suggests kernel queue alignment is a root contributor.
- Forcing runtime to prefer INT8 kernels for short prompts (length < 40) eliminated most AWQ tails at cost +6-8% CPU/GPU cost on average.
- Prefetching aggressive (prefetch full KV for next N positions) improved AWQ tails by ~15% but increased memory pressure; need limits per-GPU.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are AWQ kernel micro-launch counts a function of sequence length distribution or model layout? Need microbench per layer to confirm.
- Does tiling configuration we ship for AWQ have pathological cases for certain head counts or MLP dims? (Linnea to run per-layer microbench)
- Is there an opportunity to merge small AWQ kernels client-side in the runtime (kernel coalescing) to reduce scheduler overhead? Potential engineering cost high but high impact on tail.

Immediate next steps (owners):
- Linnea: run per-layer tiled microbench across Llama-2 variants, produce a CSV of (layer, tile_count, kernel_count, median_exec_ms) by 2028-02-24. (JIRA-REINF-4424)
- Dmitri: prototype kernel coalescing switch in runtime to batch AWQ kernel launches when microbatch count < threshold (experiment flag), target prototype 2028-03-03. (PR link in linked_artifacts)
- Miguel: evaluate adaptive batching_window (auto-grow in bursts) heuristic in the autoscaler to see SLO tradeoffs, target 2028-02-28.

Action items for product/ops:
- Recommend temporary mitigation: set kernel_preference=auto with rule: prefer INT8 for request_len<=40 for sensitive endpoints until kernel coalescing shipped.
- Add monitoring alert for p99.9 increase > 2x baseline with tag 'burst-tail-awq' to detect regressions post release.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- This aligns with a class of "queue alignment" problems we've seen before (cf. earlier kernel-scheduler jitter notes) but here memory bandwidth is the amplifying factor.
- Might be possible to design a lightweight backoff on AWQ path when DRAM bandwidth > 80% for >5ms to avoid launching more kernels that will contend. But careful: penalizing AWQ broadly removes its median advantage.
- Keep experiment logs and nvprof traces archived under /mnt/traces/burst_awq_int8_202802 for future reference.

References / context:
- Related hypos: kernel-scheduler-jitter-mixed-quant-exploration-oct2024 (see internal doc)
- Customer ticket: CS-12897 (slow chat response intermittent)

If you want raw traces/plots I can attach the links — I didn't include big PNGs in this doc. Ping on Slack (#eng-serving-runtime) if you'd like me to walk through the nvtx timeline live.

-- Asha
